blocks.content: Shared memory is the fastest form of inter process communication available on any system, because it takes a fundamentally different approach from a pipe. Rather than copying bytes through the kernel one transfer at a time, it maps the exact same physical memory pages directly into more than one process own address space, letting them read and write that memory as if it were an ordinary local variable.

This speed comes with a real responsibility the operating system does not hand out for free: shared memory provides absolutely no built in synchronization of its own, and coordinating safe access is entirely left to the processes using it, directly connecting this chapter back to the mutual exclusion ideas from the synchronization module.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409297838-333180535.png
1. Why Shared Memory Is So Much Faster Than a Pipe
blocks.text: 1. Why Shared Memory Is So Much Faster Than a Pipe

blocks.content: A pipe, covered in the previous chapter, moves data by copying it: a writer copies bytes from its own memory into a kernel buffer, and a reader later copies those same bytes back out of that kernel buffer into its own memory. Every single byte transferred crosses the kernel boundary twice.

Shared memory eliminates both of those copies entirely. Once a memory segment has been mapped into two processes address spaces, writing to it from one process and reading it from the other requires no system call at all for the actual data transfer, both processes are simply reading and writing the same underlying physical memory pages directly, exactly like accessing any ordinary variable.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409297838-149532806.png
blocks.alt: Why Shared Memory Is So Much Faster Than a Pipe

2. Setting Up a Shared Memory Segment
blocks.text: 2. Setting Up a Shared Memory Segment

blocks.content: Using shared memory follows a consistent two step pattern regardless of the specific API used. First, one process creates a shared memory segment of some requested size, which the kernel sets aside as a distinct block of physical memory not initially attached to any particular process address space. Second, each process that wants to use it, including the one that created it, explicitly attaches that segment, mapping it into its own address space at some address it can then use directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409298183-930113508.png
blocks.alt: Setting Up a Shared Memory Segment

blocks.content: 3. No Built In Synchronization: The Real Cost
blocks.text: 3. No Built In Synchronization: The Real Cost

blocks.content: The speed shared memory offers comes with a genuine tradeoff that has to be understood clearly. The operating system provides absolutely no automatic coordination between processes accessing a shared segment. If one process writes to it while another reads or writes the same region at the same time, with no external coordination at all, the result is exactly the same kind of race condition covered in full in the synchronization module, just now happening between separate processes instead of separate threads.

This is the single most important caveat of this entire chapter: shared memory gives processes the ability to touch the same data directly and instantly, but it deliberately leaves making that access safe entirely up to the processes themselves.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409298184-90535626.png
blocks.alt: No Built In Synchronization: The Real Cost

blocks.title: The single most important caveat
blocks.content: Shared memory is fast precisely because the kernel stays out of the way during actual data access. That same hands off design means the kernel also does not protect against concurrent, uncoordinated access, that responsibility belongs entirely to the application.
4. Fixing It: Pairing Shared Memory With a Semaphore
blocks.text: 4. Fixing It: Pairing Shared Memory With a Semaphore

blocks.content: The standard, correct way to use shared memory safely is to pair it with an external synchronization primitive, most commonly a semaphore or mutex from the synchronization module, that is not itself part of the shared memory segment, but governs when processes are allowed to actually touch it.

A process acquires the semaphore before reading or writing the shared region, performs its access, and releases the semaphore afterward, exactly the same mutual exclusion pattern already covered in full for threads within a single process, just now applied across separate processes instead.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409298184-214118458.png
blocks.alt: Fixing It: Pairing Shared Memory With a Semaphore

blocks.content: 5. When the Speed Actually Matters

For small, infrequent exchanges of data, the extra copying overhead a pipe imposes is genuinely negligible, and the operational simplicity of a pipe, no manual synchronization required, often makes it the better practical choice. Shared memory earns its complexity specifically when large amounts of data need to move frequently between processes.

6. Cleaning Up: Detaching and Removing a Segment
blocks.text: 6. Cleaning Up: Detaching and Removing a Segment

blocks.content: When a process is done using a shared segment, it detaches it, unmapping that memory from its own address space. Detaching, importantly, does not automatically free the underlying physical memory or destroy the segment itself, other processes may still be attached to it and actively using it.

The segment physical memory is only actually reclaimed once it has been explicitly marked for removal, typically by whichever process created it, and every process currently attached to it has detached. Forgetting this explicit removal step is a real, practical source of leaked shared memory segments lingering on a system long after the processes that used them have exited.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409298185-840469635.png
blocks.alt: Cleaning Up: Detaching and Removing a Segment

blocks.content: 7. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming shared memory automatically synchronizes access the way a pipe naturally does through its blocking behavior, when it provides absolutely no coordination of its own and requires an external semaphore or mutex.","Forgetting that detaching a shared memory segment does not remove it, the segment must be explicitly marked for removal, and can otherwise leak indefinitely.","Reaching for shared memory for a simple, infrequent exchange where a pipe operational simplicity, blocking behavior included, would genuinely be the better and safer fit."]
items: Assuming shared memory automatically synchronizes access the way a pipe naturally does through its blocking behavior, when it provides absolutely no coordination of its own and requires an external semaphore or mutex.
Forgetting that detaching a shared memory segment does not remove it, the segment must be explicitly marked for removal, and can otherwise leak indefinitely.
Reaching for shared memory for a simple, infrequent exchange where a pipe operational simplicity, blocking behavior included, would genuinely be the better and safer fit.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain precisely why shared memory is faster than a pipe, no copying through the kernel, and precisely why that same design means it needs an external synchronization primitive to be used safely, connecting directly back to the mutual exclusion concepts from the synchronization module.

Pipes and shared memory sit at opposite ends of the same tradeoff: pipes are simple and self synchronizing but pay a real copying cost, shared memory is essentially free to access but demands the application handle synchronization entirely on its own.
